extracted.intended_audience: poets and playwrights (writers of poetry and drama); teachers and students of poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Practical poetics guidance for composing verse and drama: choosing subjects, arranging parts, handling characters, language, meter, chorus, and stagecraft so works are credible, moving, and decorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a subject suitable to your abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Ye who write, make choice of a subject suitable to your abilities; and revolve in your thoughts a considerable time what your strength declines, and what it is able to support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects you can sustain: do not attempt grand themes beyond your powers. Judicious selection preserves elegance and perspicuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and simplicity of subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Be your subject what it will, let it be merely simple and uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid patchwork with conflicting episodes or wildly mixed images (e.g., a beautiful upper body terminating in an ugly fish). Keep the work coherent in idea and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incongruous and monstrous combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: so that the tame should not associate with the savage; nor that serpents should be coupled with birds, lambs with tigers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force incompatible elements together for novelty; such mixtures provoke laughter and destroy verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pompous, empty exordia and purple patch-work
rubrics_metrics.description: In pompous introductions ... it generally happens that one or two verses of purple patch-work ... are tagged on ... What will this boaster produce worthy of all this gaping? The mountains are in labor, a ridiculous mouse will be brought forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't promise more than you deliver; avoid ornate openings that do not serve the subject. Prefer fitting openings to grandiose but empty ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance concision and clarity (avoid extremes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The great majority of us poets ... I labor to be concise, I become obscure: ... he who pretends to be sublime, proves bombastical: he who is too cautious and fearful of the storm, crawls along the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscurity from over-condensation and bombast from over-ambition; aim for measured expression appropriate to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and timing of thought (arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: This ... will constitute the merit and beauty of arrangement, that the poet just now say what ought just now to be said, put off most of his thoughts, and waive them for the present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place ideas where they have most effect; delay or omit subsidiary thoughts until the proper moment to preserve tempo and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicate and cautious choice of words
rubrics_metrics.description: In the choice of his words, too, the author ... must be delicate and cautious, he must embrace one and reject another: you will express yourself eminently well, if a dexterous combination should give an air of novelty to a well-known word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise, expressive diction; a skillful recombination of familiar words often outshines needless neologisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible coinage and Greek-derived terms (sparingly)
rubrics_metrics.description: If it happen to be necessary to explain some abstruse subjects by new invented terms; it will follow that you must frame words never heard of by the old-fashioned Cethegi: and the license will be granted, if modestly used: and the new and lately-formed words will have authority, if they descend from a Greek source, with a slight deviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New words may be coined modestly and with Greek derivation to gain acceptance; avoid gratuitous or ostentatious coinage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect evolving language; custom decides usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Many words shall revive, which now have fallen off; and many which are now in esteem shall fall off, if it be the will of custom, in whose power is the decision and right and standard of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware language changes; what is proper depends on usage over time. Do not cling dogmatically to archaic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre appropriateness and decorum
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic subject will not be handled in tragic verse: in like manner the banquet of Thyestes will not bear to be held in familiar verses, and such as almost suit the sock. Let each peculiar species fill with decorum its proper place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep species distinct: match form and diction to genre, though occasional principled blending may be effective if consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional truth and pathos (move the audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough that poems be beautiful; let them be tender and affecting, and bear away the soul of the auditor whithersoever they please. If you would have me weep you must first express the passion of grief yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express genuine emotion in the performance/writing to elicit sympathy; the author must feel and show passion before expecting the audience to feel it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match voice and diction to speaker's character (decorum of speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathetic accents suit a melancholy countenance; words full of menace, an angry one; wanton expressions, a sportive look; and serious matter, an austere one. ... It will make a wide difference, whether it be Davus that speaks, or a hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor vocabulary, tone, and cadences to age, rank, temperament, education, and nationality of the speaker. Incongruent speech provokes laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency (preserve a character's nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you offer to the stage any thing unattempted, and venture to form a new character; let it be preserved to the last such as it set out at the beginning, and be consistent with itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a character's traits are established, maintain them; avoid arbitrary changes that break verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exhaustively retelling public stories; select and compress
rubrics_metrics.description: A public story will become your own property, if you do not dwell upon the whole circle of events ... nor must you be so faithful a translator, as to take the pains of rendering [the original] word for word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit what you cannot improve; focus on salient episodes and blend truth and invention so beginning, middle, and end remain consistent and engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid showing onstage things fit only for the scene behind (no implausible spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: You must not, however, bring upon the stage things fit only to be acted behind the scenes: ... Let not Medea murder her sons before the people; nor the execrable Atreus openly dress human entrails: nor let Progue be metamorphosed into a bird, Cadmus into a serpent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep onstage action credible and reportage plausible; reserve some events for reported narration to preserve believability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate dramatic length: five acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a play which would be inquired after, and though seen, represented anew, be neither shorter nor longer than the fifth act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to a five-act structure for complete and satisfying drama; avoid undue brevity or excessive length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of gods and deus ex machina only when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither let a god interfere, unless a difficulty worthy a god's unraveling should happen;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid convenient divine interventions except to resolve issues that cannot be solved otherwise without violating plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus must support action and be coherent with main design
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the chorus sustain the part and manly character of an actor: nor let them sing any thing between the acts which is not conducive to, and fitly coherent with, the main design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chorus should praise, advise, regulate passion, conceal confidences, and implore the gods—its contributions must further the play thematically and morally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modest musical accompaniment (simple flute)
rubrics_metrics.description: The flute ... slender and of simple form, with few stops, was of service to accompany and assist the chorus ... But the musician added now movements and a luxuriance to the ancient art...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple accompaniment that supports chorus and diction; excessive musical display can corrupt taste and drown dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vulgarizing heroic characters; preserve tragic dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy disdaining to prate forth trivial verses, like a matron commanded to dance ... will assume an air of modesty, even in the midst of wanton satyrs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow low buffoonery to degenerate heroic figures; maintain appropriate elevation of tragic style even amidst comic elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep satyrs/fauns appropriate — not overly urban or obscene
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fauns, that are brought out of the woods, should not be too gamesome with their tender strains, as if they were educated in the city, ... nor should blunder out their obscene and scandalous speeches. For [at such stuff] all are offended, who have a horse, a father, or an estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic/folk figures should retain rustic authenticity and avoid offensive obscenity that alienates broad audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter and rhythm: avoid overuse of spondees in iambic trimeters
rubrics_metrics.description: A long syllable put after a short one is termed an iambus ... it obligingly and contentedly admitted ... the steadfast spondees; agreeing however, by social league, that it was not to depart from the second and fourth place. But this [kind of measure] rarely makes its appearance in the notable trimeters of Accius, and brands the verse of Ennius ... with a clumsy weight of spondees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe metrical proprieties; excessive spondees produce clumsiness and weight; study Greek models for rhythmical taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be licentious because judges are unskilled
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not every judge that discerns inharmonious verses, and an undeserved indulgence is [in this case] granted to the Roman poets. But shall I on this account run riot and write licentiously?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain standards irrespective of lax critical oversight; write with care even if some readers cannot detect flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study and imitate good Greek models wisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Ye [who are desirous to excel,] turn over the Grecian models by night, turn them by day. ... if you and I but know how to distinguish a coarse joke from a smart repartee, and understand the proper cadence, by [using] our fingers and ears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the Greeks intensively and learn to discriminate fine from coarse practice; internalize cadence and repartee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good sense and knowledge of life as the foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: To have good sense, is the first principle and fountain of writing well. ... He who has learned what he owes to his country, and what to his friends ... he, [I say,] certainly knows how to give suitable attributes to every character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral and social understanding provide the material for believable characters and appropriate attributes; cultivate life-knowledge before style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance over mere ornament (matter before music)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes a play, that is showy with common-places, and where the manners are well marked, though of no elegance, without force or art, gives the people much higher delight ... than verse void of matter, and tuneful trifles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize well-observed matter and character over mere elegance or tuneful surface. Content that instructs and amuses wins audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to profit or delight, preferably both; be concise in precepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets wish either to profit or to delight; or to deliver at once both the pleasures and the necessaries of life. Whatever precepts you give, be concise; that docile minds may soon comprehend what is said, and faithfully retain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine instruction and entertainment; express teaching succinctly so it is remembered and useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid demanding belief for absurdities
rubrics_metrics.description: Let what ever is imagined for the sake of entertainment, have as much likeness to truth as possible; let not your play demand belief for whatever [absurdities] it is inclinable [to exhibit]: nor take out of a witch's belly a living child that she had dined upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain plausible imaginative limits; do not force the audience to accept blatant impossibilities without preparation or poetic justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision and patient polishing are necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you, the decendants of Pompilius, reject that poem, which many days and many a blot have not ten times subdued to the most perfect accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieving excellence requires repeated revision, erasures, and labor; do not expect masterpiece without patient polishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign parts appropriate to age and social state
rubrics_metrics.description: That the parts [therefore] belonging to age may not be given to youth, and those of a man to a boy, we must dwell upon those qualities which are joined and adapted to each person's age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cast and write parts that fit the psychological and social attributes of age and station to preserve credibility.
